title: Compute-Efficient Hyperparameter Transfer for Large MoEs
hook: Sweeping learning rates at trillion-token scale is unaffordable. Transfer across width with muP, then extrapolate along tokens with a fitted scaling law — and trust it for the real run.
key_points: Learning-rate sweeps become computationally prohibitive at extreme model size and token budget.
Step one: a Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) adaptation for MoE with Multi-head Latent Attention and the Muon optimizer, so optimal LR transfers across width.
Step two: a predictive scaling law along the token axis, fit by linear regression on small proxy runs.
Extrapolating to a 10-trillion-token horizon fits with R² = 0.95.
Validated by pretraining a 155B-total / 17B-active foundation model from scratch with the predicted configuration.
The claim: small proxy models are enough to set the learning rate for a full-scale MoE run.
content_html: Mixture-of-Experts buys capacity without proportional compute, but it doesn't make hyperparameter tuning cheaper — and at extreme model sizes and token budgets, sweeping the learning rate is simply unaffordable. Kim and colleagues propose a two-step transfer framework that answers the question with small proxy runs instead.
extra_html:
The two steps

First, they formulate a Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) adaptation for MoE architectures using Multi-head Latent Attention and the Muon optimizer, and show the optimal learning rate transfers consistently as model width scales. Second, they extend transfer along the token axis: fit a linear regression to the optimal values found by small proxy models on limited budgets, and extrapolate to very long horizons — for example 10 trillion tokens — reporting a fit of R² = 0.95.

Why it matters

The conclusion is a practical one for anyone planning a large pretraining run: proxy training on small models is sufficient to determine the learning rate for the full-scale target, turning a prohibitive sweep into a modest ablation budget. The authors back it by pretraining their own foundation model — 155B total parameters, 17B active — from scratch with the predicted configuration, and report stable training and evaluation results.

related.title: What Is a Mixture of Experts?
related.hook: Instead of running every input through one big network, route each token to a few specialist sub-networks - total capacity grows without proportional compute.

related.title: Chinchilla: Compute-Optimal Scaling
related.hook: Most giant models were starved of data. Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget you should grow parameters and tokens together — and a smaller, longer-trained model won.

related.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
related.hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.

flashcards.prompt: What are the two axes this framework transfers hyperparameters along?
flashcards.back_html: Model width — via a muP adaptation for MoE — and token budget, via a scaling law fit on small proxy runs and extrapolated to long horizons.

flashcards.prompt: What does Maximal Update Parameterization buy you here?

choices.text: The optimal learning rate found at small width stays optimal as width scales up
It removes the need for an optimizer like Muon entirely
It reduces the per-token compute cost of the MoE layers

flashcards.explanation_html: muP is a parameterization that makes optimal hyperparameters width-invariant, so a cheap small-width sweep answers the question for the large model.

flashcards.prompt: How was the method validated beyond curve-fitting?
flashcards.back_html: The authors pretrained a 155B-total / 17B-active foundation model from scratch using the predicted configuration, reporting stable training and sound evaluations.
